title: AI in Finance, Lesson 15: Building your own prompt library
subtitle: Save the prompts you use often so you never write them from scratch again.
openingQuestion: What does a prompt library give you?
openingOptions: Reuse of good prompts for the work that repeats
Freedom from ever having to verify any of the output
explanation: When a prompt produces a good result, do not let it vanish into the chat history. A prompt library is your own notebook, and each entry has five parts: the task name, when to use it, the inputs to prepare, the prompt template, and how to check the output. What separates a useful library from a messy folder is the last part - without a way to check, you are saving a trick rather than building a process.

summary.keyIdea: A prompt library is a notebook of reusable prompts for reading news, financial statements, risks and memos.
summary.commonMistake: Saving lots of prompts without recording when to use them or how to check them.
summary.action: Create your first 5 prompts for your own work.

sections.text: When a prompt works well, save it so that next time you do not start over.

sections.label: Terms
sections.text: Prompt library: where you keep reusable prompts. Fill-in template: a ready-made frame where you swap in your own information. Version: the improved copy after each round of use.
After each use, note the fault: too long, source missing, units forgotten, risks not stated. Then revise the prompt into a new version.

sections.title: The five parts of a library entry

concepts.def: Name it after the job rather than the tool. "Extract 5 metrics from the financial statements" rather than "Prompt number 3".
One line describing the situation. It lets you pick the right prompt without rereading the whole library.
Which documents, in what format, and what you need to know beforehand. Skipping this step is why a good prompt still produces poor results.
Paste it verbatim, leaving blanks such as [file name] and [reporting period] for whatever changes between uses.
The specific steps confirming the result is usable: how many figures to reconcile, which section to check. Without this part it is a trick, not yet a process.

sections.text: The improvement loop after each use

items: Record the specific fault: source missing, wrong units, conclusion stated too strongly, risks omitted, output too long.
For each fault, add exactly one constraint to the prompt - do not rewrite the whole thing.
Number the version and note the date and the reason for the change.
If a constraint is added and the fault persists, the problem is usually the input rather than the prompt.

sections.label: Two blocks worth reusing in every prompt
sections.text: The source-lock block: "Use only the attached documents; give the page, unit and period for every figure; write 'not found' where it is absent." The format block: "Answer as a table, in English, at most N words, ending with a Missing data section." These two barely change between tasks, so keep them separately and paste them in.

After a few months your library will differ from anyone else's - because it grew out of the faults you actually hit and the kind of work you actually do. That is why copying someone's ready-made prompt set and stopping there is a mistake: their set reflects their process, not yours.

lines: A prompt library turns AI tricks into a process.
A good prompt is one that has been used and revised against reality.

quiz.question: What does a prompt library mean?
options: A list of the errors AI commonly makes
The assistant's set of system rules
The assistant's store of source documents
A store of reusable prompts
quiz.explanation: A prompt library is your own store of prompts that have already worked, kept so you can run them again instead of rewriting them each time. It is not a catalogue of the model's mistakes, not the system rules that govern how the assistant behaves, and not the documents you feed it - those are the assistant's inputs, while the library is yours.

quiz.question: What should each entry carry besides the prompt itself?
options: The inputs to prepare and how to check the output
The AI model recommended for use with that prompt
The author's name and the date the prompt was created
The number of times used and the success rate
quiz.explanation: A prompt on its own is only half the recipe: without knowing what to prepare beforehand and how to check the answer afterwards, the same prompt gives a different result each time. The model name dates quickly, the author and date say nothing about whether it works, and a usage count tells you a prompt is popular rather than that it is reliable.

quiz.question: Which part of a library entry is most often forgotten and yet most important?
options: The input data required
How to check the output
The content of the prompt
The name of the prompt
quiz.explanation: Without a checking step you have only saved a trick. With one, it is a process - reusable, and handable to someone else.

quiz.question: You added a constraint to the prompt but the fault keeps recurring. Where does the cause usually lie?
options: In the prompt - it needs to be longer and more detailed
In the output format - it should be switched to a table
In the input - the document is missing or the wrong period
In the AI model - a more capable version is needed
quiz.explanation: A prompt controls how something is processed; it cannot create data that does not exist. When the constraint is clear and the fault persists, go back and check the input documents.

quiz.question: Why should each library entry carry a way of checking the result?
options: Because each prompt only works on exactly one type of document
Because this part helps the AI understand the request better and answer far more accurately
Because without a note you will later forget what the prompt was for
Because however good a prompt is, the result still has to be reconciled before use
quiz.explanation: The most easily forgotten part is precisely the part that turns a prompt into a process. Without a checking step, the library only helps you produce results faster - not know whether those results are usable.

diagram.label: A prompt produces a good result
Record all 5 parts, including how to check it
Reuse it - note the faults you find
Revise the prompt, number the version

realWorldExample.company: The first five prompts worth having
realWorldExample.description: For someone learning finance, five prompts cover most of the daily work: summarise an article as event - impact - question; extract five basic metrics from the financial statements with page references; scan for warning signs with the evidence; write a one-page memo to the five-part frame; and make the AI critique its own draft. Those five are the five preceding lessons of this stage, and what they share is a source-lock block and an output format block - the two things to keep unchanged when copying to a new task.

keyTakeaways: Each library entry has five parts, of which "how to check the output" is the most often dropped and the most important.
Number the prompt versions and record why they changed - a library is maintained, not archived.
Two components to keep unchanged on reuse: the source-lock block and the output format block.
Start with five prompts for the work you do most, rather than trying to build a large library at once.
